Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette:
Mele was a 46-year-old Tongan American musician who had spent most of her adult life performing in small ensembles, teaching voice lessons, and rehearsing in churches, studios, and community arts spaces around her city. Before she became ill, she had understood her body as reliable and finely trained; breath was part of her craft, something she could shape and trust. That changed when a severe, life-threatening respiratory illness sent her to the hospital. She remembered the most frightening moments with painful clarity: the sharp medicinal smell on the ward, the plastic dryness of oxygen tubing, the panic of trying to pull in air and feeling that each breath stopped halfway. During examinations she had to lie still while people leaned over her, and what stayed with her was not only the fear of dying but the helplessness of having to wait for someone else to tell her whether she would keep breathing.

In the months after she recovered medically, Mele found that her sense of danger had not receded. She woke in the night abruptly and sat up to check whether she was breathing normally, listening to the room and to her own chest before she could settle again. She often said that her body "went there before my mind did": a brief catch in her breath, a tight practice room, or the faint antiseptic smell in a hallway could send a jolt through her before she had even named what was happening. Gradually, safety narrowed. Home, especially her own bedroom and a single corner of the living room, felt manageable; beyond that she felt exposed, as if any unfamiliar place might become the site of another crisis.

That persistent state of alarm changed how she made sense of herself. Because she was so easily startled awake, so dependent on checking, and so quickly overtaken by physical fear, she had come to believe there was something fundamentally inadequate about her. She compared herself bitterly to the person she had been before the illness and called herself "a lousy coper," someone who should have been stronger by now. The fact that her reactions seemed to erupt automatically only deepened her self-doubt; if she could not trust herself to stay calm or to judge what was actually dangerous, then she could not trust herself to do the right thing when it mattered.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she dealt with the aftermath. When she felt weak or uncertain, she went over counterfactual versions of her life for long stretches-how different things would be if she had never gotten sick, whether she would still be taking more performance work, whether her voice would feel like her own. At harsher moments she told herself she deserved to suffer, as though her continuing fear were a kind of verdict on her character. Convinced that she did not cope well and might make the wrong decision under pressure, she began avoiding medical cues whenever she could: putting off routine physical examinations, feeling sick at the sound of ambulances, and taking elaborate routes to avoid passing the hospital where she had been treated.

Her ongoing sense of threat also pushed those habits further. Because she remained so alert to danger and trusted only a very limited set of places, avoiding hospitals and examinations felt to Mele like common sense rather than fear. If her body could react before she even thought, then why deliberately expose herself to the smells, rooms, and procedures that might set everything off? She canceled appointments, delayed follow-up care, and asked her husband to handle practical tasks that involved medical settings. The pattern had begun to affect her work. As a musician, she was repeatedly confronted by the very thing she no longer trusted: breath. In rehearsals she sometimes cut phrases short or stepped out when she noticed the slightest shortness of breath, and in older performance venues, where there might be a musty or chemical smell backstage, she became tense before going on. What frightened her most was not just the sensation itself, but the speed with which her body seized on it, making ordinary breathlessness feel like a warning.

Over time, her watchfulness seemed to make those triggers more potent. Because she was constantly scanning her breathing and waking to make sure she was safe, any small change in respiration stood out immediately. Smells linked to the hospital hit her with unusual force, and the prospect of a medical procedure felt unbearable long before it occurred. A simple exam room could feel charged from the moment she imagined it.

By the time Mele sought help, her world had become smaller than she wanted to admit. She was still teaching, but she turned down more performances, and her husband had begun urging her to get support after another night of waking in panic and checking her breath repeatedly until dawn. She came in feeling ashamed of how restricted she had become and doubtful that she could handle treatment, yet also frightened by what would happen if she kept living this way. More than anything, she wanted to trust her body enough to sing and sleep without bracing for catastrophe.
